iDevelop: Scoring and Levels

Year 6, Lesson 5

steps.label: Today's Task
steps.content:
Today's Task

Your sprites already move. Today you develop your game further by adding scoring and levels.

  • Objective: develop a program according to a plan.
  • Success criteria: develop your game to include variables.

Key vocabulary

Algorithm; plan; sprite; costume; variable; iteration (repeat, forever, wait).

This may take more than one lesson to finish properly - work at a pace that keeps your code working.

steps.label: Levels Are Backdrops
steps.content:
Levels Are Backdrops

A simple way to build a level is to change the backdrop.

  • Import or design at least two backdrops, one for each level your plan describes.
  • Switching to a new backdrop is what makes a level feel different, even if the sprites behave the same way.

steps.label: Activity 1: Add a Second Level
steps.content:
Activity 1: Add a Second Level

Work independently - use your plan to add the backdrops your game needs.

  1. Open your saved project in TurboWarp using the button.
  2. Import or design at least two backdrops for two different levels.
  3. Test that you can switch between them before moving on.

The Slides and TurboWarp switcher stays at the top right - use it whenever you need the next instruction.

steps.label: Scoring with Variables
steps.content:
Scoring with Variables

A variable is a named place that stores a value that can change while your game runs - like score.

  • Add and name a variable for the score.
  • Add and name a variable for the level.
  • Award points when your "goodie" sprite touches the "baddie" sprite.
  • Change the backdrop (level up) once the score reaches a number you choose.

options: A named place that stores a value that can change
A different look or image for a sprite
items.explain: score and level are both variables - named places that store a value which changes while the game runs.

items.prompt: In this lesson's design, what makes the game change level?
options: The backdrop switches once the score variable reaches a chosen number
The player presses a special key
The game restarts from the beginning
items.explain: Levelling up here means checking the score variable and switching backdrop once it reaches a threshold you choose.

steps.label: Activity 2: Add Score and Level
steps.content:
Activity 2: Add Score and Level

Work independently - add the variables and blocks your plan needs for scoring and levelling.

  1. Create a variable for score and a variable for level.
  2. Add a block so touching the "baddie" sprite changes the score variable.
  3. Add a block that checks the score and switches backdrop (and the level variable) once your chosen number is reached.
  4. Test after every small change - do not add everything at once and hope.

The Slides and TurboWarp switcher stays at the top right - use it whenever you need the next instruction.

Before moving on

Your score variable should change when the goodie touches the baddie, and your backdrop should change once the score reaches your chosen number.

steps.label: Easier and Harder
steps.content:
Easier and Harder

EasierAsk an adult to help you understand what a variable is for and where to add the blocks that use it.
HarderAdd a third level, and make the game harder (for example, faster) each time the level changes.

steps.label: Testing Your Code
steps.content:
Testing Your Code

Look back at what you actually built today, then answer honestly - this is marked by you, not a computer.

items.prompt: What did you name your score variable and your level variable, and what does each one store?
items.modelAnswer: Names the two variables and says what each one is tracking (for example: score counts points from touching the baddie; level tracks which backdrop should be showing).

items.prompt: Why did you test after each small change today, rather than waiting until score, level and the backdrop switch were all added?
items.modelAnswer: If something breaks and you only test at the end, it could be any of the blocks you added. Testing each small change means you already know it must be the piece you just added, so bugs are much faster to find - next lesson (iDebug) builds on this.

Think about how many blocks you would have to check if you only tested at the very end.
